explanations.answer: He looks this way and that
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says Moses looked "…this way and that…" and saw no one (Exodus 2:12). He checks around before he does anything else. I think this is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't hurry past it.

explanations.answer: He calls out to the guards
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions guards, friend. It says Moses looks "…this way and that…" and sees no one (Exodus 2:12). That look is the first thing we're told he does.

explanations.answer: He waits for it to stop
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any waiting, baker. It says that after Moses looked "…this way and that…" and saw no one, he struck down the Egyptian (Exodus 2:12). The looking comes first, and then he acts.

Sand, baker. Moses looked this way and that, saw no one, struck down the Egyptian and hid the body in the sand (Exodus 2:12). This is a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly. And watch what happens next: the very next day a Hebrew asks him, "Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" (Exodus 2:14).
Reeds do show up in Moses' story, friend, but earlier. His basket was placed among the reeds along the bank of the Nile (Exodus 2:3). Here the text says he hid the body in the sand (Exodus 2:12).

No river in this verse, friend. After looking this way and that and seeing no one, Moses hid the body in the sand (Exodus 2:12). This is a heavy moment, so I'll keep it simple. It turns out the secret didn't stay buried, because Moses thought, "This thing I have done has surely become known." (Exodus 2:14).

Right on target, baker. Moses asks the one in the wrong, "Why are you attacking your companion?" (Exodus 2:13). He doesn't put the question to the other man. The text says it was the next day when Moses went out and saw two Hebrews fighting, and this time he speaks up.

The text doesn't say who was losing, friend. It says Moses asked the one in the wrong, "Why are you attacking your companion?" (Exodus 2:13). That word "attacking" tells us whose behavior he was asking about. I can't even referee two people reaching for the last cookie, so I respect the nerve.

The text never gives their ages, baker. It only says Moses asked the one in the wrong, "Why are you attacking your companion?" (Exodus 2:13). Nothing about who was older. Sometimes the whole answer is already in the verse.

You got it, baker. The man says, "Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" (Exodus 2:14). He doesn't just push back on Moses. He brings up the Egyptian right alongside asking who made Moses ruler and judge. I think that question lands like a dropped tray of cookies, and everybody in the kitchen hears it.

explanations.answer: The palace Moses grew up in
explanations.explanation: The man never mentions a palace, friend. He asks, "Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" (Exodus 2:14). The Egyptian is what he brings up. I think that's what rattles Moses.

That's not in the man's reply, baker. After asking who made Moses ruler and judge, he says, "Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" (Exodus 2:14). The Egyptian is what he brings up. Labor never comes into it.
True, baker. The text says, "Then Moses was afraid…" (Exodus 2:14). The man's words hit him hard. Moses thought the thing he had done had surely become known.

The text says the opposite, friend. It says "Then Moses was afraid…" (Exodus 2:14). Right after the man's words, Moses thinks the thing he has done has surely become known. I think Moses felt the floor shift under him.
That's not what the text says, baker. When Pharaoh heard about it, "…he sought to kill Moses." (Exodus 2:15). Nothing slides here. Moses was right to be afraid.
False is right, baker. The text says Pharaoh "…sought to kill Moses." (Exodus 2:15). Word got to the top of Egypt, and the king did not shrug it off. That's why Moses ran.
Midian, baker! Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian (Exodus 2:15). That's where he sat down beside a well. Keep that well in mind, because the next scene gathers around it.

Close in sound, friend, but the text names a different land. Moses "…settled in the land of Midian…" (Exodus 2:15). Midian is where the well is. Keep that name handy, because the story stays there a while.
The text doesn't send him there, baker. It says Moses fled from Pharaoh and "…settled in the land of Midian…" (Exodus 2:15). Midian is the name to hold on to. It's where the next scene happens.
Not this time, baker. When the shepherds drove the daughters away, "…Moses rose up to help them…" (Exodus 2:17). He doesn't stay out of it. He's a man who steps in when he sees trouble.

False, baker! The text says Moses "…rose up to help them…" when the shepherds came along and drove the daughters away (Exodus 2:17). He doesn't stay out of it. He had been sitting beside that well (Exodus 2:15), and now he gets up to step in.

Watered, baker. Shepherds drove the daughters away, and Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock (Exodus 2:17). Look at the switch, though. First he's sitting beside a well in a brand new land (Exodus 2:15). Then somebody needs help, and he's up and pulling water. I know that feeling. I once sat in a drawer for years, and the second somebody needed me, I was ready to work.

Sheared? Friend, nobody pulled out the clippers at that well! The daughters came to draw water and fill the troughs (Exodus 2:16), and Moses watered their flock (Exodus 2:17). Water was the whole job. If somebody had handed me shears, I'd have stamped a sheep and called it a day. Wrong tool, wrong chore.

Nobody counts sheep here, baker. The text says Moses rose up to help the daughters "…and watered their flock." (Exodus 2:17). Water is the job he helps with. Seven daughters, one flock and a well make for plenty of work.

explanations.answer: Why they're home so early today
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Reuel, the priest of Midian, asks, "Why have you returned so early today?" (Exodus 2:18). He noticed the timing first. Seven daughters walking in ahead of schedule will get any dad's attention.

explanations.answer: Why they didn't fill the troughs
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Reuel asking that, friend. Reuel, the priest of Midian, asks, "Why have you returned so early today?" (Exodus 2:18). His question is about the time. The troughs aren't the issue.

explanations.answer: Why they left the flock behind
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the text, baker. Reuel, the priest of Midian, asks his daughters, "Why have you returned so early today?" (Exodus 2:18). He's asking about how early they are. The flock isn't what he brings up.
Look again, baker. The daughters say, "An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds…" (Exodus 2:19). They call him an Egyptian, not a Hebrew. That's the word they used.

False, baker. The daughters tell their father, "An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds…" (Exodus 2:19). They say Egyptian, and that's how they describe him. They also say he drew water for them and watered the flock.

explanations.answer: Invite him to have something to eat
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Reuel says, "Invite him to have something to eat." (Exodus 2:20). He asks them to bring the man in for a meal. A good host knows what to do when someone has helped his family.

explanations.answer: Pay him for watering the flock
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention pay, friend. Reuel says, "Invite him to have something to eat." (Exodus 2:20). The response he asks for is a meal. Nothing about money.

explanations.answer: Send him safely back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: That isn't what Reuel says, baker. He tells his daughters, "Invite him to have something to eat." (Exodus 2:20). The text doesn't mention sending Moses anywhere. He's being asked in, not sent off.
Zipporah is right, baker. Reuel gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage (Exodus 2:21). A meal invitation turned into a wedding. That's quite a result from showing up at a well.

Leah is a real Bible name, friend, but she's from another story. She was the woman brought to Jacob in the evening (Genesis 29:23). Here the text says Reuel gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses (Exodus 2:21). Easy to mix up, so no worries.

Rebekah belongs to another story, baker. She became the wife of Isaac, Abraham's son (Genesis 24:67). Here the text says Reuel gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses (Exodus 2:21). Z-i-p-p-o-r-a-h is a long one, so I get it.

explanations.answer: He's become a foreigner in a foreign land
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses names his son Gershom, saying, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land." (Exodus 2:22). He has a wife and a son now, and he still says that about himself. I think those words have some ache in them.

explanations.answer: He's finally found a home in a new land
explanations.explanation: That's not what Moses says, friend. He names his son Gershom, saying, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land." (Exodus 2:22). He calls himself a foreigner. I think there's a lot packed into that one line.

explanations.answer: He'll never go back to Egypt again
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Moses say that, baker. When he names Gershom, he says, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land." (Exodus 2:22). That's all he says about himself. It tells us how he sees his place in Midian.

Yes, baker. The text says "…their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God." (Exodus 2:23). Their groaning goes up to God Himself. The Israelites cried out under their burden of slavery, and the cry went to Him.

The text sends the cry somewhere else, friend. "…their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God." (Exodus 2:23). Moses is off in Midian and the verse never says the cry reaches him. It goes up to God.

The text puts the cry somewhere else, baker. It says the king of Egypt died, and then "…their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God." (Exodus 2:23). The verse names God as where it went. Hold on to that direction.

True, baker. The text says, "God saw the Israelites and took notice." (Exodus 2:25). Right before that, God heard their groaning and remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 2:24). The people were noticed.

The text says the opposite, friend. "God saw the Israelites and took notice." (Exodus 2:25). Right before that, "…God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." (Exodus 2:24). He saw them, and He took notice.
